checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are EIP-7825 and EIP-7883 activated simultaneously at Fusaka fork?

state_context: BeaconChainConfig is an immutable singleton after initialization. FuluForkEpoch is the sole consensus-layer activation flag for the entire Fulu/Fusaka fork bundle. EIP-7825 and EIP-7883 are execution-layer EIPs activated within the Fusaka fork by the EL client (go-ethereum).

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The BeaconChainConfig struct contains a single FuluForkEpoch field that activates the entire Fulu/Fusaka consensus fork. There are no separate EIP-7825 or EIP-7883 fields in the consensus layer configuration. The FuluEnabled() function trivially checks FuluForkEpoch < math.MaxUint64. The initForkSchedule function builds a deterministic, ordered fork schedule with one Fulu entry. No state inconsistency is achievable within Prysm for this property.
state_anomalies_found: EIP-7825 and EIP-7883 are absent as individually trackable flags in BeaconChainConfig; no separate activation state exists.
FuluForkEpoch could theoretically be configured out-of-order relative to ElectraForkEpoch in YAML, but newNetworkSchedule sorts entries by epoch.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: BeaconConfig() is an immutable singleton after initialization. No cache inconsistency is possible for fork epoch fields.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent access risk. BeaconChainConfig is read-only after node startup.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No symbolic path in Prysm branches on EIP-7825 vs. EIP-7883 state. The only relevant variable is FuluForkEpoch. No counterexample is constructable within Prysm's codebase. EIP activation consistency between CL and EL is maintained by shared YAML configuration and Engine API epoch parameters.
attack_scenarios: Misconfigured network with mismatched CL/EL Fusaka fork epoch: caught at Engine API level through newPayload rejections, not a Prysm code vulnerability.
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. Fork activation is determined at startup from static config.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: FuluForkEpoch is set from trusted YAML configuration files at node startup. It is not modifiable via P2P, RPC, or any attacker-controlled input during runtime. No external attacker can influence the value of FuluForkEpoch.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No external attack surface. Config is loaded from local trusted files.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant 'EIP-7825 and EIP-7883 activate simultaneously at Fusaka' is an EL-level invariant, not a CL-level invariant. Prysm correctly implements its side of this: the Fulu fork epoch activates the Fulu consensus rules. EL enforcement of EIP-7825/7883 is delegated to the EL client (geth) and is architecturally separate from Prysm's responsibilities.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: FuluForkEpoch field in BeaconChainConfig, used by FuluEnabled() and initForkSchedule()
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for Prysm's CL scope. Not applicable to EL EIP activation (by design).
edge_cases: CL/EL fork epoch mismatch in deployment configuration: caught at Engine API boundary, not a Prysm code bug.
FuluForkEpoch < ElectraForkEpoch in config: would cause fork schedule disorder, but sorted at schedule construction time.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: EIP-7825 and EIP-7883 are execution-layer gas cap changes activated within the Fusaka (Fulu) fork by the EL client. Prysm's consensus layer has no separate toggles for these EIPs by design. The CL correctly activates the Fulu fork at FuluForkEpoch. EL activation consistency is enforced through the Engine API newPayload/forkchoiceUpdated handshake. No vulnerability exists within Prysm for this check item.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No code change needed in Prysm. Deployment documentation should specify that the CL FuluForkEpoch must match the EL Fusaka activation block. Prysm could optionally add a startup warning if the connected EL reports an incompatible fork configuration via the Engine API exchange capabilities.

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Do MEV-Boost relays validate gas cap for submitted blocks?

state_context: registrationCache is in-memory and populated by RegisterValidator calls. After node restart, the cache is empty until validators re-register. BoltDB fallback also returns ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient for unregistered validators. Both error types trigger the gas limit validation bypass.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The getPayloadHeaderFromBuilder function skips all gas limit validation when RegistrationByValidatorID returns any error, including the common ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient (validator not registered locally). This is not a transient error case; it is the expected state for validators that use a relay without submitting local registration. The error-handling path logs a warning and accepts the builder bid with whatever gas limit the relay chose.
state_anomalies_found: Gas limit validation is entirely bypassed when RegistrationByValidatorID returns ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient or ErrNotFoundRegistration — the most common non-error states for unregistered validators.
No rejection path exists when gas limit cannot be verified; the code accepts the bid unconditionally.

In proposer_builder.go, the same ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient and ErrNotFoundRegistration errors are explicitly handled as valid 'not registered' cases (returning false, nil), but in proposer_bellatrix.go they are treated as generic errors that bypass validation.
The registration cache can be empty (e.g., after node restart before registration re-submission), creating a systematic window where gas limits are unvalidated.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: registrationCache is an in-memory store populated by RegisterValidator calls. After node restart, the cache is empty until validators re-register. During this window, all builder bids bypass gas limit validation. The BoltDB fallback (when registrationCache is nil) also returns ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient for unregistered validators, triggering the same bypass.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent access race identified in this specific validation path. The bypass is a logic flaw, not a race condition.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: A malicious relay targeting a validator with no local registration can submit bids with arbitrary gas limits (bounded by EL's 1/1024 per-block deviation rule), bypassing Prysm's gas limit check. Multi-block gradual gas limit drift is not caught by any CL guard.
phase2_symbolic_execution.counterexample: Validator V uses relay R. V has no local registration in Prysm (ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient). Relay R returns a bid with GasLimit = parentGasLimit + parentGasLimit/1024 - 1 (maximum allowed by EL deviation rules). Prysm skips gas limit validation (logs warning), accepts bid, produces block. Repeated over N blocks: gas limit drifts by up to (1 + 1/1024)^N factor without any CL detection. Over 720 blocks (~3 hours), gas limit can approximately double.
attack_scenarios: Single-block maximum deviation: relay returns a bid with gas limit at the maximum EL-allowed deviation. CL accepts without validation. EL accepts (within 1/1024 rule). No CL detection.

Multi-block gradual inflation: relay consistently returns bids at parentGasLimit + parentGasLimit/1024 - 1. Over ~1024 blocks, gas limit approximately doubles. This could inflate block gas limits, enabling MEV strategies requiring high gas throughput.
Multi-block gradual deflation: relay returns bids at parentGasLimit - parentGasLimit/1024 + 1. Gas limit gradually deflates to relay-desired lower bound.

Post-restart attack: during the registration re-propagation window after node restart, all validators building with MEV-Boost lack local registrations; gas limits are unvalidated for all builder bids during this window.
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: No specific timing required beyond the validator lacking a local registration. Most effective immediately after node restart before registration re-submission.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The MEV relay endpoint (GetHeader call) is fully attacker-controlled if the relay operator is malicious or the relay is compromised. The registration lookup is internal. Any validator that uses MEV-Boost but has not submitted registration to this specific Prysm instance (or after a node restart) is vulnerable to this bypass.
entry_points: MEV relay GetHeader RPC response (attacker-controlled if relay is malicious)
Node restart clearing in-memory registrationCache before re-registration
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: MEV relay endpoint returns builder bids including GasLimit field. When the local validator registration is absent, Prysm accepts any GasLimit value from the relay without validation.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant 'builder bid gas limit must equal expectedGasLimit(parentGasLimit, reg.GasLimit)' is explicitly violated whenever RegistrationByValidatorID returns an error. The guard is absent on the error path. The EL-side deviation rule provides partial mitigation for large single-step attacks but does not prevent gradual multi-step gas limit manipulation.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: RegistrationByValidatorID error check with warning log and continue path (lines 258-266 of proposer_bellatrix.go)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Insufficient. The guard only validates gas limits when registration lookup succeeds. It does not reject bids when validation cannot be performed. The EL 1/1024 rule provides partial defense but is insufficient against gradual drift.
edge_cases: Node restart: registrationCache is empty; all builder bids bypass gas limit validation until validators re-register.
Validator uses relay but never registered with this Prysm node: permanent bypass of gas limit validation for that validator.
DB I/O error (transient): would also bypass validation, though less likely to be exploitable on demand.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: A malicious or compromised MEV relay can submit builder bids with unvalidated gas limits when the proposing validator has no local registration. This is exploitable from an external, attacker-controlled interface (the relay endpoint). The gas limit manipulation is bounded by the EL's 1/1024 per-block rule, but gradual multi-block drift is undetected by Prysm. The severity is moderated by the EL-side partial mitigation and the requirement for a malicious relay, but the bug class (safety-critical validation bypass with external trigger) qualifies for bug bounty consideration.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Change error handling in getPayloadHeaderFromBuilder (lines 258-266 of proposer_bellatrix.go): distinguish between ErrNotFoundFeeRecipient/ErrNotFoundRegistration ('not registered' — use parentGasLimit as fallback expected gas limit or reject the bid) vs. other errors (reject bid). Remove the unconditional bypass. This is consistent with how proposer_builder.go:45 handles these same error types.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.severity_estimate: Medium (bounded by EL-side mitigation, but systematic bypass of a safety-critical check via attacker-controlled input)

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does block validation catch private channel txpool bypasses?

state_context: The CL/EL architectural split explicitly delegates all transaction-level validation to the execution layer. Per-tx gas caps (EIP-7825) are enforced by the EL client (geth) via newPayload INVALID responses. The CL gossip validator is not designed to inspect individual transaction properties within the execution payload.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The validateBeaconBlockPubSub function validates beacon blocks at the gossip layer with checks for blob count, slot timing, proposer signature, proposer index, and execution payload timestamp and parent optimistic status. It does not inspect individual transactions within the execution payload, their gas values, or per-transaction gas caps. This is by architectural design: the CL/EL split delegates all transaction-level validation to the execution layer. No state anomaly exists within Prysm's design for this property.
state_anomalies_found: No ValidatePayloadHeader function exists in beacon-chain/core/blocks/payload.go for per-transaction gas cap checking (audit item itself notes this function does not exist).
validateBellatrixBeaconBlock validates only version, execution enabled, timestamp, and parent optimistic status — no transaction-level properties.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: Block validation state (seen blocks, pending queue, bad blocks) is tracked but these are block-level, not transaction-level. No cache inconsistency affects per-tx gas cap enforcement.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: validateBlockLock (line 65-66) serializes gossip block validation. No concurrency issue relevant to this property.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: A block containing transactions violating EIP-7825 (per-tx gas cap) passes all checks in validateBeaconBlockPubSub. The block is accepted at gossip layer and propagated. The EL then rejects it via newPayload INVALID response. The attack succeeds in broadcasting an invalid block but fails to extend the canonical chain.
phase2_symbolic_execution.counterexample: A valid proposer (controlling their validator key) submits a beacon block via gossip with an execution payload containing a transaction with gas = blockGasLimit (violating EIP-7825). validateBeaconBlockPubSub accepts the block (all CL checks pass). Block is broadcast. EL processes via newPayload, returns INVALID. Block is invalidated at state transition level, not at gossip validation. The block propagates but does not extend the canonical chain.
attack_scenarios: Malicious proposer broadcasts a block with EIP-7825-violating transactions: propagated by Prysm gossip, rejected by EL newPayload. Result: wasted network bandwidth but no canonical chain impact.

Private channel (Flashbots Protect) includes a transaction violating EIP-7825 in a builder bid: relay would fail newPayload, causing the proposer's block to be invalid. Strong economic disincentive discourages this.
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. The attack path is deterministic given a valid proposer and EIP-7825-active EL. The block propagates before EL rejection.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The gossip network is fully accessible to any network peer. However, submitting a block with an EIP-7825-violating transaction requires controlling a validator's signing key (to produce a valid proposer signature). While the gossip layer propagates the block, the EL provides the definitive rejection via newPayload. This is the intended architecture.
entry_points: P2P gossip (libp2p pubsub) — accessible to any network peer with a valid proposer key
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: P2P gossip layer accepts the block, EL newPayload rejects it. The CL gossip layer is not the enforcement boundary for per-tx gas caps by design.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant 'CL gossip validation catches private channel txpool bypasses (EIP-7825 violations)' is not an intended invariant of the Prysm codebase. The CL/EL architecture places per-transaction validation at the EL layer. Prysm's validateBeaconBlockPubSub correctly implements all CL-layer gossip validation requirements per the Ethereum consensus specification.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: EL newPayload INVALID response for EIP-7825-violating transactions
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: The EL newPayload guard is sufficient and is the architecturally correct enforcement boundary for EIP-7825. CL gossip validation is not expected to duplicate EL transaction validation.
edge_cases: Before Fusaka activation: EIP-7825 does not apply; per-tx gas caps are not enforced by either CL or EL. Correct.
After Fusaka activation: EL enforces EIP-7825 at newPayload time.
A block producer building locally submits an EIP-7825-violating transaction: the EL rejects the transaction at getPayload time before it ever enters a block.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The absence of per-transaction gas cap validation in Prysm's CL gossip validator is not a vulnerability — it is the correct implementation of the CL/EL split architecture. Transaction-level validation (including EIP-7825 per-tx gas caps) is delegated to the execution layer and enforced via newPayload. Private channel transactions are subject to identical EL-level validation as public mempool transactions. Prysm correctly implements all CL gossip validation requirements.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No code change required in Prysm. EIP-7825 enforcement is the responsibility of the EL client. Documentation could clarify that per-tx gas cap enforcement for MEV-Boost paths occurs at EL newPayload time.
